column2: The Great Porn Experiment | Gary Wilson | TEDxGlasgow
column5: Worth knowing before you watch: TED attached a note to this one saying some claims aren't well supported by the medical literature. Doesn't make it worthless, it's the talk that got a lot of people thinking about this at all, but treat it as a starting point rather than settled science. If a specific claim here matters to you, go look up the study behind it.

column2: Pornography Isn't Your Problem | Jason Mahr | TEDxCincinnati
column5: The reframe is the useful part. If porn is the coping mechanism rather than the problem, the question stops being "how do I resist harder" and becomes "what am I coping with." Practical version: for a week, don't try to quit, just write down what you were feeling in the ten minutes BEFORE, not during. The pattern usually shows up fast.

column2: Why I stopped watching porn | Ran Gavrieli | TEDxJaffa
column5: Fair warning that this is more an ethics-and-values talk than a how-to. He's making an argument about what porn does to how we see people, not handing you a quitting method. Useful for the "why" if your motivation keeps evaporating, but pair it with something practical.

column2: Changing the narrative around the addiction story | Cameron Staley | TEDxIdahoStateUniversity
column5: This is essentially ACT applied to compulsive behaviour, and the distinction he draws matters: moving toward something you value holds up better than moving away from something you hate about yourself. Shame-driven streaks tend to snap. Values-driven ones bend.

column2: Escaping Porn Addiction | Eli Nash | TEDxFortWayne
column5: The thing he lands on is the thing most people skip. Secrecy is load-bearing here, and it stays load-bearing until you tell one actual human being. Not the internet, not a comment section, one person who knows your name. That single conversation does more than most apps.

column2: Let's Talk Porn | Maria Ahlin | TEDxGoteborg
column5: Useful one for parents and teachers specifically. It's about porn as a cultural and educational problem rather than an individual's habit, so if you came looking for personal recovery steps this isn't that, but it's a good primer on what kids are actually walking into.

column2: Why we need to talk about porn | Jo Robertson | TEDxChristchurch
column5: She works in this professionally in New Zealand and it shows. Good one to send to a parent who wants to have the conversation but has no idea how to open it. The core point is that silence isn't neutral, kids just fill the gap with whatever they find.

column2: Healing Addictive Behaviors: My Porn Story | David Norwell | TEDxSurrey
column5: This is a personal story rather than a method, which is worth knowing going in. Stories are genuinely useful for the "I'm not the only one" part, which is not nothing. But if you're trying to actually change something this week, watch it and then go find something structured.

column2: How porn is destroying young men | Gary Wilson (Key Points Talk)
column5: Heads up that the framing is strong and the underlying science is contested. There are researchers who'd push back hard on the "destroying" part. Watch it, then watch someone who disagrees, and notice which one is arguing from evidence and which from certainty. That's a useful skill in this whole genre.

column2: Rethinking Porn: Why Shame, Not Sex, Is the Problem | Paulita Pappel | TEDxMunchen
column5: Genuinely valuable as a counterweight to most of what's in this space. Her argument is that distress often comes from the conflict between the behaviour and your beliefs rather than the behaviour itself. You don't have to agree with all of it, but if shame is the loudest part of your experience, this is worth sitting with.

column2: Porn The New Tobacco | Jack Fischer | TEDxBinghamtonUniversity
column5: The tobacco analogy is rhetorically strong but it does break down, and it's worth noticing where. Nicotine has a measurable physical dependency profile that this doesn't. That doesn't mean the behaviour isn't a problem for people, just that borrowed metaphors can smuggle in claims nobody has actually tested.

column2: We Need To Talk About Sex Addiction - Paula Hall - TEDxLeamingtonSpa
column5: Paula Hall is an actual clinician who treats this, which makes this one different from most talks in the genre. If a talk has convinced you that you want help but you don't know what "help" looks like, she's a good bridge to understanding what therapy for this actually involves.

column2: Growing Up in a Pornified Culture - Gail Dines - TEDxNavesink
column5: Worth setting expectations: this is a sociological and feminist critique of porn culture, not clinical advice about compulsive use. Two different conversations that get tangled a lot. Both are legitimate, but if you're here for help with your own habit, this isn't aimed at you.

column2: 6 Dangerous Stages of Porn Addiction
column5: Stage models like this are useful as a map and unhelpful as a verdict. Most people don't move cleanly through numbered stages, and deciding you're at "stage 5" mostly just adds dread. Use it to notice direction of travel, not to diagnose yourself.

column2: How to Overcome Porn Addiction
column5: The five-step framing is fine, but the step people skip is the boring one: making it physically harder. Not because willpower is fake, but because willpower is a limited budget and you shouldn't spend it on a decision you could have removed entirely. Phone out of the bedroom does more than any mindset shift.

column2: Pornography Addiction and Treatment Strategies
column5: Good playlist if you want something structured rather than the algorithm handing you a random video whenever you're already struggling. That last part matters more than it sounds. Watching recovery content at 1am mid-urge is usually just a different way of staying in the loop.

column2: Breaking the Cycle of Pornography (Porn) Addiction
column5: One thing worth adding: the cycle described here usually has a quieter step before the obvious one. Boredom, or a small rejection, or being tired. If you only start paying attention at the urge, you're already very far downstream. The intervention point is earlier than it feels.

column2: Urologist Explains how to break the cycle of porn addiction
column5: Useful to hear this framed medically rather than morally. A urologist talking about it as a functional issue tends to land differently for people who've tuned out the shame-based version entirely, which is a lot of people.

column2: THIS VIDEO WILL END YOUR PORN ADDICTION (Breaking Free From Addiction)
column5: No single video ends anything, and that's not a criticism of this one, it's just worth saying out loud. The realistic version is that a video can give you one idea you actually use. If you watch this and change nothing by tomorrow, the problem isn't that you need a better video.

column2: How to Stop Porn Addiction (Never Relapse Again)
column5: "Never relapse again" is a promise nobody can keep, so hold that part loosely. The useful frame is that relapse is data rather than verdict. What you do in the 48 hours afterwards matters far more than the slip itself.

column2: Am I Addicted to Porn? What is Porn Addiction?
column5: Self-assessment is helpful but hold it loosely. Frequency alone tells you very little. The questions that actually discriminate are whether it's escalating, whether you've tried to stop and couldn't, and whether it's eating things you care about. Those three matter more than a number per week.

column2: How to Quit Porn Fast - The 3 Brain Recovery Stages
column5: Stage models for recovery are more useful than stage models for addiction, because at least you're measuring something you're building. Just don't expect the stages to arrive on schedule. Most people ping-pong between two of them for a while before anything settles.

column2: How to Kick Your P**n Habit in 35 Minutes
column5: Anything promising a fix in a fixed number of minutes is selling the decision, not the change. Which can still be worth something, honestly, a lot of people are stuck at the deciding stage. Just know that's the bit being addressed here.

column2: If you can't quit p*rn, this is for you
column5: If you're watching this because you've tried and failed several times, the useful reframe is that repeated attempts are how this usually goes, not evidence you're incapable. Most people who eventually stop have a long string of failed attempts behind them. That string is part of the process, not a separate thing.

column2: WARNING - Po*n Addiction is Destroying You - 5 Ways to STOP it NOW! Ashu Ghai
column5: Fear-based motivation works for about a fortnight and then stops. Worth knowing that going in, because when it stops working people assume they've lost their motivation permanently. You haven't, you just used up the fuel that particular tank holds.

column2: How to Stop Porn Addiction - Dopamine Hijack
column5: "Hijack" is a decent metaphor but it can make you feel like a passenger in your own head, which isn't helpful. The system is doing exactly what it evolved to do with an input it never evolved for. You're not broken, you're well-adapted to the wrong environment.

column2: How to Quit Porn Permanently
column5: "Permanently" is doing a lot of work in that title. A more honest target is that it stops being the thing organising your week. Plenty of people get there. Fewer get to a state where the thought never crosses their mind again, and aiming for that mostly just creates fresh failure conditions.

column2: Quit Porn Addiction (playlist)
column5: Playlists are underrated for this, mainly because they stop you from doom-searching. One practical note: watch these at a time when you're fine, not at the moment you're struggling. Building understanding and managing an urge are different jobs.

column2: How to Finally Quit Porn (playlist)
column5: Good playlist. General tip for this whole genre: pick one source and go deep rather than sampling twenty. The advice contradicts itself across creators and the contradictions will paralyse you more than any single piece of mediocre advice would.

column2: Quit any addiction - The Easypeasy way to quit the p*rn
column5: The Easypeasy approach borrows heavily from Allen Carr's smoking method, which is worth knowing because it tells you the mechanism: it's trying to dismantle the belief that you're giving something up. Works well for some people and does nothing for others. Worth a try since it costs you an afternoon.

column2: Get Rid Of Porn Addiction (playlist)
column5: Another playlist for the collection. Quick practical note: if you find yourself with six recovery playlists saved and no actual change, that's a recognised pattern. Consuming content about the problem can become its own comfortable substitute for addressing it.

column2: How to Quit Porn
column5: Straightforward title, straightforward video. If you want one thing to do after watching: pick the single easiest friction point to add and do it now rather than planning a system. Tonight's version of you needs an obstacle, not a strategy.

column2: How to Quit Porn Addiction? Control Your 5 Senses & Take Back Your Mind
column5: The sensory-control angle is essentially attention management, which is a reasonable frame. Where it gets practical is noticing that the decision usually happens before the conscious decision, in the fifteen minutes of aimless scrolling nobody counts as part of the episode.

column2: Break Free Porn Addiction (playlist)
column5: Playlist rather than a single video, useful if you want to work through in order. Worth keeping a note of which specific ideas you actually tried, because after a dozen videos they blur and you'll swear you've tried everything when you've mostly just watched everything.

column2: You Will NEVER Watch P*RN Again
column5: Absolute statements like this are motivating right up until the first bad night, at which point they become evidence you've failed completely. If you take anything from a video like this, make it a direction rather than an absolute, because the absolute version is fragile in exactly the moment you need it not to be.

column2: What Is Porn Addiction? BlockP
column5: Useful as a plain definitional overview if you're at the "is this even a thing" stage. Worth knowing the terminology is genuinely unsettled: "porn addiction" isn't a formal diagnosis, though ICD-11 does recognise compulsive sexual behaviour disorder. Different clinicians will frame the same situation differently.

column2: When does watching porn become an addiction?
column5: This is the right question and the honest answer is that there's no clean line. Most practitioners look at loss of control, escalation, continued use despite consequences, and distress. Notice that "how often" isn't really on that list. Two people at identical frequency can be in completely different situations.

column2: The Hidden Roots of Porn Addiction
column5: Root-cause framing is useful as long as it doesn't become a reason to postpone. You can work on the underlying stuff and reduce the behaviour at the same time, and for most people the second one makes the first one easier, not harder. Waiting until you've fully understood yourself is its own kind of avoidance.

column2: Quit Porn & Rewire Your Brain In ONLY 16 Weeks | NoFap Reboot
column5: Sixteen weeks is a plausible ballpark and also completely made up for you specifically. Some people feel meaningfully different in three weeks, some in eight months. The number is useful as "this takes a while, settle in" and unhelpful as a deadline you can fail.

column2: The 2 STEP PROCESS To Quit Porn & Reboot Your Brain | NOFAP SUCCESS
column5: Two-step frameworks are always a bit tidy for something this messy, but the general shape is right. The part worth underlining is that the second step, replacing rather than just removing, is what determines whether month three holds. Removal alone leaves a hole and the hole gets filled.

column2: CHANGE YOUR BELIEFS To Quit Porn & Reboot Your Brain | NOFAP SUCCESS
column5: Belief change is slower than behaviour change and that's worth knowing upfront. You'll probably act differently before you feel differently about yourself, and there's a gap in between where it feels fake. That gap is normal, not evidence it isn't working.

column2: 7 Things You Can Do To SPEED UP NoFap Recovery | NoFap Reboot Faster
column5: Sleep is the item on lists like this that people skip and shouldn't. Tiredness wrecks impulse control more reliably than almost anything else, and most relapses cluster late at night for exactly that reason. Fixing your bedtime is unglamorous and does more than most of the rest of it.

column2: How much does a relapse set back your porn reboot?
column5: Good question to have answered honestly. The "back to zero" framing is the genuinely harmful bit of streak culture. Whatever changed over six weeks does not evaporate in one evening, and treating it like it does is what turns one slip into a fortnight.

column2: Porn Reboot NoFap Flatline: How to Make NoFap Better with Dr. Trish Leigh
column5: Flatline is the part nobody warns people about, and then it arrives and they assume they've broken something. Worth knowing it's a commonly reported phase, it's temporary for most people, and it is not a reason to "test" whether things still work.

column2: How To SPEED UP Your Porn Reboot With ONE DAILY HABIT
column5: Single-habit advice is usually oversold, but the underlying logic holds: one thing you do daily regardless of mood beats an elaborate system you abandon in week two. Doesn't hugely matter which habit. Matters a lot that it's small enough to survive a bad day.

column2: 3 Tips To RECOVER From A PMO RELAPSE | NoFap FAILED Again
column5: The most useful thing after a relapse is boring: what happened in the two hours before. Not self-analysis about your character, just the actual sequence. Tired, alone, scrolling, bored. You're collecting data on a pattern, not building a case against yourself.

column2: How long will it take to reboot my brain from porn?
column5: Honest answer is that nobody can give you a real number, and anyone who does is guessing. Rough consensus is weeks to months for most of the noticeable stuff, longer for some. Frustrating answer, but a made-up precise one is worse.

column2: What Can Happen If You DON'T QUIT PORN & REBOOT YOUR BRAIN (NOFAP FAIL)
column5: Consequence-focused videos work best as a nudge for people still deciding, and badly as fuel for people already trying. If you're already in it, dwelling on worst cases tends to raise anxiety, and anxiety is a trigger. Know which of those two you are before pressing play.

column2: NoFap's Alexander Rhodes explains how porn addiction is impacting a generation
column5: Interesting historically regardless of what you make of NoFap as a community. He started it as a forum thread and it became a very large support network, with all the good and bad that implies. The peer support is real; some of the physiological claims that grew up around it are not well supported.

column2: Your Brain Rebalanced Radio S02E05: Alex Rhodes (NoFap founder) and Mark Queppet
column5: Good listen if you want the origin story rather than advice. Also a decent illustration of how fast an internet community generates its own folklore, some of which is genuinely useful and some of which is just confidently repeated until it sounds like fact.

column2: Alexander Rhodes (playlist)
column5: Playlist rather than a single video. Worth remembering when working through community-founder content that founders are advocates, not neutral summarisers. Useful perspective, just not the one to rely on for whether a specific claim holds up.

column2: Porn Addiction Coach - Noah Church
column5: Coaching content is worth evaluating the same way you'd evaluate a therapist: what's the actual method, what happens if it doesn't work, and is there anything they'd tell you they can't help with. Good ones answer all three. Be a bit wary of ones that don't.

column2: How & Why To Stop Watching Porn with Noah B.E. Church
column5: He's open about starting young and about the erectile issues, which is the part a lot of men won't say out loud and then assume they're uniquely broken. Hearing someone name it plainly is often the thing that finally gets people to a doctor.

column2: Noah B.E. Church Interview, Author of 'Wack: Addicted to Internet Porn'
column5: If the book is what brought you here, the short version is that it's a first-person account rather than a clinical text. Useful for recognition, less useful as a treatment plan. Both kinds of thing have a place, just know which one you're holding.

column2: Noah B.E. Church (channel)
column5: Channel rather than a single video. Reasonable one to subscribe to if you want a steady drip of this rather than binge-watching six hours of recovery content in one night, which, speaking practically, is usually a form of procrastination.

column2: How Porn Hooks Your Brain - The Addiction Loop Explained
column5: Short and accurate enough on the loop. The bit worth adding is that the loop isn't only about pleasure, it's about anticipation. The seeking is the sticky part, which is why endless scrolling and tab-opening can feel more compulsive than whatever you're supposedly scrolling toward.

column2: Part 4: Dopamine: The Molecule of Addiction | Your Brain on Porn | Animated Series
column5: Solid on dopamine, and one correction to how this usually gets repeated: dopamine isn't the pleasure chemical, it's closer to the wanting chemical. That distinction explains the very common experience of compulsively doing something you're not even enjoying anymore.

column2: #033 - Porn Addiction: Dopamine, Disgust, and Erectile Dysfunction (Gary Wilson)
column5: Long-form conversation rather than a quick explainer, so save it for when you've got the time. The erectile dysfunction section seems to change behaviour most, probably because it's concrete and immediate in a way "your reward system" isn't.

column2: How Porn Addiction Rewires Your Brain and Destroys Intimacy, Doctor Explains
column5: Worth separating two claims that get blurred here: that heavy use can affect arousal to real partners, which has some evidence, and that it rewires your brain permanently, which is overstated. First one's worth taking seriously. Second one just adds fear without adding a plan.

column2: Porn Addiction Is Not About Sex - Neuroscience Explained
column5: The title's doing some heavy lifting but the point underneath is sound. For most people this isn't primarily about sexual desire, it's about regulating something else. If you've ever done it while not remotely in the mood, you already know this is true.

column2: Why Porn Is Addictive: Dopamine And Brain Chemistry Explained
column5: Decent explainer. One thing to watch for across this whole category: brain-scan language sounds authoritative and is easy to overstate. "Lights up" is not a finding. If the science is what convinces you, it's worth learning to read it a bit sceptically.

column2: Part 1-5: Your Brain on Porn | Animated Series (full)
column5: Useful compilation if you want the whole animated series in one sitting. Fair warning that the underlying model is Gary Wilson's and it's disputed by a chunk of the research community. Good explanation of a particular theory rather than a neutral summary of the evidence.

column2: Part 1: Introduction | Your Brain on Porn | Animated Series
column5: Good entry point to the series. Animated explainers are genuinely useful here because the mechanism is abstract, and abstract things are easier to dismiss when they're just words on a screen.

column2: Part 2: The Coolidge Effect | Your Brain on Porn | Animated Series
column5: The Coolidge effect is real and well documented in animals, and the leap to human internet use is the contested part. Worth watching and worth noticing exactly where the argument moves from observed data to plausible-sounding extension.

column2: Part 3: The Reward Circuit | Your Brain on Porn | Animated Series
column5: Reward circuitry explained clearly enough for a general audience, which is harder than it looks. If you've been told "it's just a bad habit" and that never quite fit your experience, this is a decent counterweight.

column2: Part 5: Pornography Addiction Test | Your Brain on Porn | Animated Series
column5: Self-tests are best used as a conversation starter with an actual professional rather than as a diagnosis. Bear in mind there's no formally recognised "porn addiction" diagnosis in the DSM, though ICD-11 does include compulsive sexual behaviour disorder. That distinction matters if you're seeking treatment.

column2: Your Brain On Porn (Animated Summary) | Gary Wilson
column5: Good summary version if you don't want the full series. As with all of these, worth pairing with one critical source so you're not getting a single model presented as consensus.

column2: Your Brain on Porn by Gary Wilson - Book Summary
column5: Book summaries are handy but they flatten the caveats, and this is a topic where the caveats are most of the argument. If the summary convinces you, read the actual thing, and ideally read something that disagrees with it too.

column2: Remembering Gary Wilson of Your Brain On Porn: My Friend & Hero
column5: Wilson died in 2021. Whatever you make of his conclusions, he did get a lot of men to talk about something they were carrying silently, and that part stands independently of how the science eventually shakes out.

column2: Part 3: The Reward Circuit | Your Brain on Porn in Urdu | Animated Series
column5: Good to see this translated. Access is a real barrier in this space, most of the decent material is English-only, so subtitled and translated versions genuinely matter for people who'd otherwise have nothing.

column2: Gary Wilson | Your Brain On Porn (Episode 158)
column5: Longer interview format, which suits this better than a ten-minute video. Worth listening to the whole thing rather than clipping it, because the qualifications he adds are usually in the parts that don't survive short-form edits.

column2: The Mechanism of Addiction - Your Brain on Porn - Animated Series Part 1-8
column5: Handy if you want the extended cut. One general note on animated explainers: the clarity is the selling point and also the risk, because a clean diagram can make a contested hypothesis look like established mechanism. Enjoy the clarity, keep the uncertainty.

column2: Porn Addiction Is Misunderstood: How To Actually Stop - Dr. K Healthy Gamer
column5: The genuinely useful reframe is that the behaviour is often solving something. That's not permission, it's a direction. If you remove the solution without addressing what it was solving, you've made your week worse and changed nothing structural.

column2: Helping Viewers with Porn Addiction
column5: Live-call format, which makes it more useful than a lecture for a lot of people. Hearing someone describe the exact thing you thought only you did is a specific kind of relief that reading about it doesn't replicate.

column2: Why Pornography Addiction is MISUNDERSTOOD (It's NOT What You Think) With Dr K
column5: He's a psychiatrist, and the "misunderstood" part is mostly aimed at the fear-based version of this conversation. If you've bounced off the moralising takes, this is a more clinical framing that might actually land.

column2: The Neuroscience Of Porn Addiction: How To Actually Stop - Dr. K Healthy Gamer
column5: Good on the mechanism. The practical takeaway buried in the neuroscience is that reducing cue exposure beats increasing resistance, every time. You are not going to out-discipline a feed built by people who are very good at their jobs.

column2: Dr. K Healthy Gamer Talks About Porn Addiction
column5: Worth watching alongside his other videos on this. He's fairly careful about not overclaiming, which is unusual for the genre and makes the claims he does make more credible.

column2: Sexuality and Porn | Healthy Gamer (playlist)
column5: Playlist covering the broader sexuality material rather than just compulsive use, which is a useful distinction. A lot of distress in this area is actually about shame around ordinary sexuality, not about compulsion at all.

column2: How your diet combats p**n addiction
column5: Diet framing is a stretch as a direct causal link, but there's a real indirect version: blood sugar crashes, poor sleep and low energy all degrade impulse control. Not magic. Just the unglamorous physical baseline doing a lot of quiet work.

column2: Biggest Predictor Of P*rn Addiction | Dr K Healthy Gamer
column5: Worth noting predictors are population-level statistics, not verdicts on individuals. Useful for understanding risk in general, useless for predicting what you specifically can do. Don't read a statistic as a sentence.

column2: The Science Of Screen Addiction & How To Stop - Dr K Healthy Gamer
column5: Broader screen-addiction framing, which is often more useful than treating porn as an isolated category. For a lot of people it sits inside a general pattern of using a screen to not feel something, and treating only one branch leaves the trunk.

column2: The Porn Addiction Crisis No One Wants to Talk About - Dr. K
column5: The "nobody wants to talk about it" framing is a bit overdone by now given how much content exists, but the substance is solid. He's a psychiatrist and it shows in how carefully he hedges.

column2: Can Pornography Cause Erectile Dysfunction? | Top Tips to Naturally Reverse ED
column5: If this brought you here because of an actual erectile problem, please also see a doctor. Porn-related causes are plausible, and there are also cardiovascular and hormonal causes that need ruling out. Those are the ones where delay actually costs you something.

column2: Porn-Induced Erectile Dysfunction Is Real - Joe Rogan Was Right About NoFap
column5: Fair to note this remains genuinely contested among researchers rather than settled. The honest position is that many young men report it, the mechanism is plausible, and the evidence is weaker than confident videos imply. Worth taking seriously and worth not catastrophising.

column2: Day 13: Porn-Induced Erectile Dysfunction: How to Heal It w/ Dr. Trish Leigh
column5: Practical thing not always said clearly enough: if you're rebooting and worried about function, the anxiety itself becomes a major contributor. Performance anxiety is a well-established cause of ED entirely on its own, and monitoring yourself for signs of recovery feeds it.

column2: The Truth Of Porn Induced ED (PIED) - Dr. Trish Leigh
column5: Worth pairing with an actual urologist's take. Neuroscience framing is useful, but ED has a differential diagnosis, and "it's the porn" is a conclusion you should reach by elimination rather than assumption.

column2: Can Watching Porn Cause Erectile Dysfunction? - Doctor Explains
column5: Good to have a doctor answering this plainly. The short version most medical sources land on is that it's possible, probably less common than the internet suggests, and worth investigating properly rather than self-diagnosing from YouTube.

column2: Porn Induced Erectile Dysfunction - Dr. Kelkar (MD) Psychiatrist
column5: Useful to have this in Hindi and from a psychiatrist. Language access is a genuine gap here, and a lot of people get their entire understanding of this from whatever happens to exist in their language, accurate or not.

column2: The Truth About Porn-Induced Erectile Dysfunction (From a Sex Therapist)
column5: Sex therapists tend to give the most grounded take on this because they see the full range, including the many cases where porn isn't the cause at all. Good corrective if you've only been consuming recovery-community content.

column2: How To Overcome Porn Induced Erectile Dysfunction
column5: The bit worth holding onto is that recovery of function, when porn is genuinely the driver, tends to be gradual and non-linear. Expecting a switch to flip on a particular day sets you up to read a normal bad night as total failure.

column2: Is Porn The Reason For Your Erectile Dysfunction? The Science Explained
column5: Reasonable overview. If you take one thing: whether to masturbate without porn during a reboot is a genuinely open question among people who work in this, and you'll find confident opposite answers. Don't let one creator's rule become something you feel guilty about breaking.

column2: Porn Induced Erectile Dysfunction - New Age of Tech
column5: Reasonable framing of it as a modern-conditions problem rather than a personal defect. Unlimited novelty on demand is genuinely new, and it's fair to notice human arousal systems didn't evolve with it in mind, without concluding you're broken.

column2: Coach Noah Church on How to Recover from Porn-Induced ED
column5: Coach rather than clinician, which is worth knowing when weighing the advice. Not a knock, there's plenty of useful lived-experience knowledge in this space, just a different thing from clinical training and worth being clear which you're getting.

column2: How to CURE a porn addiction? - Doctor Explains
column5: "Cure" is the wrong word for most behavioural stuff and it sets a strange bar. Management that holds for years is the realistic and genuinely good outcome. Framing it as cure-or-failure is how people talk themselves out of counting real progress.

column2: Porn Addiction Therapy Treatment And Recovery
column5: Useful if you're deciding whether to seek treatment at all. One thing worth knowing: you don't need to meet some threshold of severity to justify seeing someone. "This bothers me and I'd like it to stop" is a sufficient reason.

column2: Pornography Addiction Recovery: The Basics
column5: Aimed at clinicians but genuinely useful for anyone who wants to know what treatment actually involves rather than what it's imagined to involve. Demystifying it makes people more likely to go.

column2: TREATING PORNOGRAPHY ADDICTION
column5: Worth knowing the clinical picture is contested. Some practitioners treat this as an addiction, some as a compulsivity issue, some as primarily a shame-and-values conflict. Those lead to different treatments, which is a good thing to ask about before committing to one.

column2: Pornography Addiction EXPERT Shares Top Relapse Prevention Strategies
column5: Relapse prevention is the part people skip because it's less exciting than quitting, and it's the part that determines whether any of it lasts. Making a plan for the bad night while you're having a good day is the whole trick.

column2: Break the Cycle of Pornography Addiction | Ryan Soave & Dr. Andrew Huberman
column5: Soave's background is in treatment programmes and it shows in how practical this is. The shame section in particular is worth the time, because shame is the mechanism that converts one slip into a week.

column2: What Porn Addiction Recovery Actually Looks Like
column5: Good honest title. The gap between what people imagine recovery looks like and what it actually looks like causes a lot of unnecessary quitting. It's mostly unremarkable and occasionally hard, not a dramatic arc.

column2: Therapist Reveals the Relationship Between Adult Entertainment and Addiction
column5: Short but the point stands. Therapists who work in this generally see far more shame-related distress than clinical compulsion, which is a genuinely important distinction for how you approach your own situation.

column2: Porn Addiction: Treatment Without Shame (Clip)
column5: The without-shame framing matters more than it sounds. Shame reliably predicts worse outcomes, not better ones, which is counterintuitive if you grew up believing that feeling bad enough is what makes you stop.

column2: Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder ICD-11
column5: Useful for anyone who wants the actual diagnostic language rather than internet terminology. CSBD is in ICD-11, it is not the same as "porn addiction," and the criteria centre on failure to control impulses over time plus real-world harm. Handy to know if you're talking to a clinician.

column2: Dr. Stephanie Carnes discusses Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder
column5: Stephanie Carnes works in this clinically and the precision is the value here. If you've only encountered this topic through recovery creators, hearing how it's actually defined and assessed in practice is a useful recalibration.

column2: Sex and Pornography Addiction - Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Recovery
column5: CBT is the approach with the most evidence behind it for compulsive sexual behaviour, so it's good to see it explained properly rather than repackaged as a mindset hack. The homework is the active ingredient, not the insight.

column2: How CBT Can Help You Overcome Porn Addiction?
column5: Good plain explanation. The part worth internalising is that CBT isn't about arguing yourself out of urges, it's about changing what you do in the gap between trigger and action. That gap is trainable even when the urge isn't.

column2: From Dependence to Freedom - A Clinical Perspective on Pornography Addiction Recovery
column5: Clinical framing rather than motivational, which suits some people much better. If every video you've watched has felt either preachy or hyped, something written for practitioners can be a relief.

column2: Overcoming Porn Addiction (playlist)
column5: Playlist rather than a single video. If you're working through a structured set like this, one suggestion: keep a note of the specific techniques you actually attempted, because otherwise a month later it feels like you've tried everything when you've mostly just listened.

column2: Integrating CBT, ACT & Mindfulness Based Therapy for Substance Use Disorders
column5: Broader than porn specifically, which is the point. Compulsive behaviours share a lot of machinery, and treatments developed for substance use often transfer. Useful if your situation involves more than one thing, which is common.

column2: Escape the Grip of Porn Addiction - 10 Powerful Recovery Tips
column5: Lists of ten tips are only useful if you pick one. Genuinely, pick one, do it for two weeks, then come back for the next. The reason these lists don't work isn't that the tips are bad, it's that nobody implements ten things at once.

column2: The 3 Stages of Porn Addiction Recovery
column5: Stage models for recovery are more forgiving than stage models for addiction, but the same caveat applies: expect to move back and forth rather than forward. Regression between stages is standard and isn't a sign the process failed.

column2: How To Stop Relapse In Porn Addiction Recovery
column5: Worth pairing with something on what to do after, not just before. Most practical relapse-prevention work is really two plans: one for reducing the odds, one for keeping a slip from becoming a fortnight. The second is the one people never write down.

column2: Inpatient Sex Addiction Treatment Centers - Dr. Doug Weiss
column5: Inpatient is a big step and worth knowing it exists, though it's aimed at a narrow slice of severity. For most people reading this, outpatient therapy or a group is the proportionate option. Knowing the full range makes it easier to pick honestly.

column2: Paradise Creek Recovery Center (channel)
column5: Treatment-centre channels are worth watching with the obvious caveat that they're also marketing. That doesn't make the clinical content wrong, plenty of it is solid, just read it knowing there's a service at the end of the funnel.
